rows.narration: Your hands are mirror images. This year's Nobel Prize in Chemistry is about how one hand can take over.

rows.visual: Blur-dissolve match cut from the hands to ball-and-stick L-alanine (from PubChem CID 5950 coordinates) and its mirror image made by NEGATING x across the dashed line (never a 180° rotation); element letters C, N, O, H so the four different groups read; the orange one stays crisp, the mirror one fades to faint hatched teal; margin note "your proteins: one hand only"

rows.narration: Many molecules come in two hands like that. Life is picky: your proteins use only one hand of each amino acid.

rows.narration: Yet a reaction left to itself makes both hands, fifty-fifty. A one-handed catalyst, a helper that isn't used up, can tip the balance.

rows.visual: A notebook page headed "Frank's recipe · 1953", margin note "Charles Frank, theoretical physicist"; three hand-drawn checkboxes write on, each on its word: "1 a one-handed catalyst", "2 boost one hand, hold back the other", "3 a reaction that makes its own catalyst"; box 1's tick lands on "early nineteen hundreds" with the label "early 1900s"; labels "Kagan, 1986" and "Soai, 1995" appear next to boxes 2 and 3 late in the shot (ink, >= 3.5% of frame height); tiny source note "numbered as in the Nobel popular background"

rows.narration: In nineteen fifty-three, Charles Frank wrote a recipe for one hand to take over completely. One: a one-handed catalyst; chemists had that by the early nineteen hundreds. Two: boost one hand and hold back the other. Three: a reaction that makes its own catalyst.

rows.visual: Two parts with an in-shot page turn. 5a (~12.5 s): box 2's tick draws; margin note "Henri B. Kagan · 1986"; our own drawing of a metal disc "M" holding two pieces; "pieces 75 : 25"; three pairs as a pie: orange-orange 56%, grey mixed 38%, teal-teal 6% (exact 56.25/37.5/6.25 % of the circle); the mixed slice struck through in INK with "barely works"; the pie re-splits to "working catalysts 90 : 10"; credit "numbers from Nobel figure 4 · our drawing". 5b (~7 s): hand-ruled chart, axes "catalyst pieces: lead" and "product: lead"; dashed straight line "what a straight line predicts" and a solid orange curve bowing above it; "shape only, not Kagan's data"

rows.narration: In nineteen eighty-six, Henri Kagan ticked box two. His insight: the catalyst's metal holds two pieces, so mixed hands make three kinds of pairs, and the mixed pair barely works. Start seventy-five to twenty-five, and the working catalysts are ninety to ten: a purer product than a straight line predicts.

rows.narration: In nineteen ninety-five, Kenso Soai ticked box three: a molecule that helps build more of itself, same hand, from simple ingredients.

rows.narration: In two thousand three, his team started with a lead of five parts in ten million. Each run's product seeds the next: fifty-seven percent after one run, ninety-nine after two, past ninety-nine and a half after three.

rows.narration: Then, with no one-handed ingredient added, the reaction still picked a hand, at random. In thirty-seven runs, nineteen leaned one way, eighteen the other.

rows.visual: Label top-left for the whole shot: "our toy model · trend only" (+ small "Frank-type model, 10,000 runs"). Two-colour dots racing in a flask (one real toy run from race_runs.json), then a histogram of the final lead building run by run (histograms.json counts; first_400_bin for the first second, then ease to 10,000): "copying only" -> FLAT; a notebook switch "+ box 2: mixed pairs stop working" flips on (a grey pair forms, as in shot 5) and the histogram morphs into two tall spikes at the ends, orange solid / teal hatched; counters "4,951" and "5,049"; a small coin flips between the spikes. x-axis "final lead: ← all mirror hand · all one hand →"

rows.narration: In our toy model, copying alone isn't enough: ten thousand runs end up anywhere. Add box two, where a one-hand and a mirror molecule pair up and stop working, and nearly every run ends with one hand taking over. Which hand is a coin toss.

rows.visual: The spikes shrink to a corner; a hand-written boxed quote: “not an answer to the origin of biological homochirality” (Nobel Committee, on Frank's model); below: "How Soai's reaction works: two competing explanations (Nobel background)"

rows.narration: A toy, not how life chose its hand. The Nobel Committee stresses Frank's model isn't the answer to life's origin, and how Soai's reaction works is still debated.

rows.narration: Choosing the hand matters for medicines: one form does the job, and its mirror image can cause unnecessary, sometimes harmful, side effects.
